pages.p: A **variable** is a named box that stores a value. Make one with the keyword «let», then a name, then «=» and the value. The «=» sign means "store this", not "is equal to" like in maths.
pages.tip: Making a variable is called **declaring** it. A keyword is a special word that JavaScript already knows.

pages.p: A variable created with «let» can get a new value later. Write the name and «=» again, without «let». JavaScript remembers only the latest value. You can use the old value to make the new one.

pages.h: const: a box that stays shut
pages.p:
Use «const» for a value that should never change. If you try to give it a new value, JavaScript stops with a «TypeError».

Good habit: start with «const». Use «let» only when the value really has to change.
pages.tip: Writing «planet = "Mars";» later would cause the error «Assignment to constant variable».

pages.p:
A name can have letters, digits, «_» and «$». It cannot start with a digit. It cannot have spaces or dashes. Names are case-sensitive: «score» and «Score» are different. You also cannot use keywords like «let» or «const».

For names with several words, JavaScript programmers use **camelCase**: «firstName».
pages.tip: Pick names that explain the content: «totalPrice» is better than «x».

pages.p:
Every value has a **type**:

• **number**: 7, -3, 3.14 (whole numbers and decimals are the same type)
• **string**: text in quotes, like «"hi"»
• **boolean**: «true» or «false»

The word «typeof» tells you the type of a value.
«"5"» is text and «5» is a number. They behave differently. With two numbers, «+» adds. With two strings, «+» **joins** them.
pages.tip: Quotes can be single, double, or backticks. The value is a string in all three cases.

pages.p:
Two special values mean "no value":

• «undefined»: JavaScript uses it when a variable has no value yet.
• «null»: you use it when you want to say "empty on purpose".
Use «Number()» to turn text into a number and «String()» to turn a value into text. This matters when text arrives from somewhere else, like a form on a web page.
pages.tip: Converting does not change the original variable. It gives you a new value.

pages.p: A **template literal** is text between backticks «`». Inside it, «${...}» puts a value or a small expression into the text. It is easier than joining many pieces with «+».
pages.o:
Zoe is 12 years old
Next year: 13
pages.tip: The backtick key is usually next to the number 1 or below Esc.

pages.p: A string has built-in tools. Write a dot, then the tool name. «length» counts the characters. «toUpperCase()» and «toLowerCase()» change the case. A tool that does something is called a **method**, and it has round brackets.
pages.tip: «length» has no brackets. Methods like «toUpperCase()» always do.

pages.p: «slice(start, end)» cuts out a piece of text. Counting starts at **0**. It includes the start position but not the end position. «includes(text)» answers «true» or «false». It is case-sensitive.
pages.tip: With only one number, «slice» goes from there to the end.

pages.p:
«trim()» removes spaces from both ends. It is useful for text typed by people.

An important fact: methods never change the original string. They give back a **new** one. Save it in a variable if you need it.

hand.q: Which keyword makes a variable whose value can change later?
hand.why: «let» creates a variable that you can assign again. «const» cannot be changed, and «int» belongs to other languages.
The new value is built from the old one: 5 + 2 = 7.

hand.q: Which is a valid variable name?
hand.why: Names cannot start with a digit, and cannot contain spaces or dashes. Digits are fine after the first character.
«typeof» gives the type name in lowercase. A value in quotes is a string.

hand.q: Complete the template literal so it prints Hello, Zoe!
hand.why: Inside backticks, «${name}» is replaced by the value of the variable.
Both values are strings, so «+» joins them instead of adding.

hand.q: Put the lines in order to print 7.
hand.why: The variable must exist first. Then it changes, and only then do we print its latest value.
«toUpperCase()» gives a new string with all letters in capitals.
A variable declared without a value holds «undefined».
«slice(0, 4)» takes positions 0, 1, 2 and 3. The end position is not included.
«Number("42")» turns the text into the number 42, so «+» adds.

hand.q: Complete the method so the line prints true.
hand.why: «includes» checks whether the text contains the piece we give.

hand.q: What happens if you assign a new value to a «const» variable?
wrong: JavaScript silently ignores the new value
The variable turns into a «let» variable
hand.why: A constant cannot be reassigned. JavaScript reports a TypeError, which protects you from changing it by mistake.

hard.why: «last.slice(0, 1)» is only the first letter. The dot after the closing brace is plain text.
After «trim()» only «hi» is left. Its length is 2. The spaces are gone.
One side is a string, so «+» joins instead of adding. The number 3 is turned into text.
The quotes make «"5"» a string. «5» is a number, and «true» is a boolean.
«toUpperCase()» returns a new string. We did not save it, and the original is unchanged.
Whatever is inside «${ }» is worked out first, then its result is put in the text.
Only «true» without quotes is a boolean. In «a» and «c» the quotes make strings.
«includes» is case-sensitive. «Pineapple» contains «apple» with a small a, not «Apple» with a capital A, so the answer is false.

hard.q: Print the first three letters in capitals: MON.
hard.why: «slice(0, 3)» gives «mon», and then «toUpperCase()» changes that piece to «MON».
«String(n)» makes the text «12». Two strings joined with «+» give «1212», not 24.

items.why: A «const» can never get a new value. Use «let» for values that change.

items.symptom: It prints Hi, ${name}! instead of Hi, Zoe!
items.why: «${ }» only works inside backticks. Single quotes make plain text.
«"20"» is a string, so «+» joins it with 5. «Number()» makes it a real number.

items.symptom: It does not print HELLO. It prints something about a function.
items.why: A method needs round brackets to run. Without them you only point at the method.
A variable name cannot start with a digit.

items.symptom: It prints false, but the sentence mentions pizza.
items.why: «includes» is case-sensitive: «pizza» and «Pizza» are different pieces of text.

project.title: Username Maker
project.brief:
Write a function «username» with two inputs, «first» and «last» (both text, they may have extra spaces at the ends).

It must return the first 3 letters of the first name followed by the first 3 letters of the last name, all in lower case. Remove spaces at the ends first. If a name has fewer than 3 letters, use all of it.

Example: «username("Ada", "Lovelace")» returns «"adalov"».
